node.label: Deborah Gray White
node.date_label: Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985; revised 1999) · Too Heavy a Load (1998; paperback 1999) · Telling Histories, ed. (2008)
node.description: In Ar’n’t I a Woman? Female Slaves in the Plantation South (1985), Deborah Gray White argued that slavery must be understood through enslaved women’s work, reproduction and relationships with other women, rather than treating men’s experience as universal. She examined how racial and sexual stereotypes concealed women’s vulnerability and the networks through which they sustained family and community life. Too Heavy a Load (1998) extended White’s analysis to Black women’s organizing and the conflicts among racial solidarity, gender and class; Publishers Weekly praised its systematic focus but judged its textbook structure and tone unlikely to reach lay readers. Her edited Telling Histories (2008) examined Black women’s place in the historical profession, and the collective Scarlet and Black project, coedited with Marisa J. Fuentes (2016), brought institutional slavery research into Rutgers’s public history.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ar’n’t I a Woman? Female Slaves in the Plantation South (1985; revised edition 1999); Too Heavy a Load: Black Women in Defense of Themselves, 1894–1994 (1998; paperback 1999); Telling Histories: Black Women Historians in the Ivory Tower (editor, 2008); Scarlet and Black, Volume 1: Slavery and Dispossession in Rutgers History (coeditor with Marisa J. Fuentes, 2016); Lost in the USA (2017).
node.scope_note: White’s monographs, complete Telling Histories essays and Scarlet and Black chapters remain unread. Argument evidence comes from White’s interview and article abstract, named reviewers, publisher descriptions and Morgan’s published acknowledgment. hooks’s chapter was read in its complete journal-published Turkish translation; the English original remains unread. The 1983 article’s displayed notes and the licensed 1994 anthology preview were read, but its full article/chapter body was not.

proposed_edges.relationship: White and Marisa J. Fuentes coedited Scarlet and Black, Volume 1: Slavery and Dispossession in Rutgers History (2016), a collective investigation of Rutgers’s institutional past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher page: title/editor credits; publication details, 20 December 2016; description; complete contents. Credits say “Edited by” both scholars; White separately wrote the introduction. Chapter findings belong to their named authors. Chapters unread; neither sole authorship nor personal intellectual influence is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: White served on the board of senior editors for Black Women in America, second edition (2005), edited by Darlene Clark Hine alongside a larger editorial team.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Thompson’s participant-authored page, final Black Women in America section: Hine is editor; White is listed on the “Board of Senior Editors.” The roles are distinct. Rutgers also names their collaboration but gives 2004; the participant’s edition date is 2005. Entries unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985) made enslaved women’s productive and reproductive labor central to explaining slavery’s place in American history, an emphasis White restates in her Rutgers interview.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lamiell interview, first question and White’s first answer: slavery was sustained “through the wombs” of African American women as well as their labor. Intro identifies the 1985 book. The displayed 1969 date is invalid and unused. Full monograph unread; retrospective testimony supports this contribution.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Female Slaves” (1983), White argued that women’s resources and cooperation created a partly autonomous female world and matrifocal family relations within plantation slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher abstract, sentences on work/resources, female cooperation and conclusions; short phrase “slave families were matrifocal.” Abstract only, not a fresh reading of the article body. Its 1994 reprint is separately identified in Half Sisters of History; no universal account of all slave societies is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: White’s edited Telling Histories (2008) used Black women historians’ autobiographical essays to examine exclusion and the making of the profession, a contribution Linda Wynn identifies in her 2010 review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wynn review: paragraph introducing seventeen contributors; paragraphs beginning “Engagingly written” and “Even though the essayists.” She explains the collection’s historiographical value and questions of researcher identification. Full collection unread; this is attributed review evidence, with White’s editorial role preserved.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Fuentes and a collective of researchers, White’s Scarlet and Black (2016) brought Rutgers’s involvement in slavery into public institutional history and framed that research as a resource for the university’s future.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description’s final paragraph calls the collective history “a usable one”; contents credit White’s reconciliation introduction. Coeditor and contributor credits read. Chapter bodies unread. This projects White’s documented role alongside the existing Fuentes-to-public-history route; it does not duplicate that edge or attribute all findings to either editor.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her introduction to Telling Histories (2008), Deborah Gray White extends Darlene Clark Hine's argument that twentieth-century Black women developed a culture of dissemblance as a defense against rape, suggesting that the same mindset was one of the factors that kept educated Black women from writing anything but celebratory history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed introduction excerpt through its final, truncated paragraph. Immediately after note 19, White names Hine’s explanation of protective concealment and then writes, “I suggest that this same conscious and unconscious mindset”, applying it to historical writing. The proposed debt concerns that application alone. The continuation and Hine’s underlying essay were not read. This differs from the existing encyclopedia editorial credit.
